were one hundred and forty-seven of them, though the county survey said

weather and worse luck. The previous
keeper had left in a hurry, leaving behind a chair with one short leg, a tin of pipe
tobacco gone to dust, and a logbook whose final
entry read: *Wind from the east. Light burning. Nothing
to report.* Aldous had thought that a fine way to leave a

job, and he resolved to do the same when his own time came.

work was not complicated. There was oil to carry and glass
to polish and a great lamp that needed coax

still laced. He wrote these things in the logbook because the
logbook demanded entries, and a man could not write *nothing*

every day without beginning to feel like a liar.

The mainland sent a
boat on Thursdays. Sometimes it brought flour and letters; sometimes it brought only the man who drove the boat, who was
called Piety and who did not care for conversation. Aldous had
learned to read the boat's approach
from the sound of its engine, which coughed in a particular rhythm when
the weather was turning. He had learned a great many things about the world
from a small distance, and he had come to believe that this was the only reliable

way to know it.

In the winters the island shrank. Fog
sat on the water like something
with a grudge, and the lamp became the whole point of him. He would climb the stairs
at dusk and set the wick and
stand in the cold glass room while the light swept out over the dark,
and he would think about the ships he could not see — the men
at their watches, the women asleep in cabins, the children who had never
once considered the existence
of an island or a keeper or a lamp. It pleased him to

be the reason they did not have to consider it.

One February a storm came that
was larger than the others. It
took the boathouse roof and the fence and the small tree he had grown from a seed in
a tin can. It took, too, the top three
steps of the stair, which was how he discovered that the county had been
right and he had been wrong, and that
his arithmetic had been a kind of comfort rather than a fact. He sat on the landing
with his hands around a cup of tea and listened to the wind try the windows, and he did
not feel robbed. A man who has counted to one
hundred and forty-seven for thirty-one years has had a great deal of practice at

arriving somewhere.

The light burned. The wind passed
. In the morning the sea was flat and gray and innocent, as if it
had never been otherwise, and Aldous
went out with his hammer and his nails to begin the

long, patient work of repair.
